content: Vector-borne diseases exhibit seasonal patterns due to the relationship between rainfall and the availability of breeding sites for vectors. Temperature and relative humidity are also critical factors, as they influence the geographical distribution of vectors, particularly by altitude and latitude. Travelers in urban areas generally face a lower risk of exposure to certain vector-borne diseases, especially if they stay in air-conditioned accommodations. However, they remain at risk of exposure to Aedes mosquitoes, which are vectors for dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses. These mosquitoes are prevalent in urban centers of tropical countries and are primarily active during the daytime. In rural areas or regions with poor hygiene and sanitation, travelers are at a higher risk of exposure to disease vectors. Personal protective measures are essential in such settings. Outdoor activities during the evening and nighttime can increase the risk of exposure to malaria vectors. To protect against vector-borne diseases, travelers can use insect repellents, which are substances applied to exposed skin or clothing to prevent contact with vectors. Repellents should be used strictly according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and the recommended dosage should not be exceeded, particularly for young children and pregnant women. The active ingredients in repellents repel insects but do not kill them. Travelers should select repellents containing DEET (N,N-diethyl-3-methylbenzamide), IR3535 (3-[N-acetyl-N-butyl]-aminopropionic acid ethyl ester), or icaridin (1-piperidinecarboxylic acid, 2-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-methylpropyl ester). Repellents should be applied during times when insects are actively biting, and care must be taken to avoid contact with mucous membranes. Repellents should not be sprayed on the face, applied to the eyelids or lips, or used on sensitive, sunburned, or damaged skin. Hands should be washed after application. In hot and humid climates, where sweating is profuse, reapplication may be necessary every 3–4 hours. Mosquito nets provide excellent protection during sleep. Nets can be used with or without insecticide treatment, but treated nets are significantly more effective. Pre-treated nets are commercially available. The net should be tucked under the mattress, ensuring it is not torn and that no mosquitoes are inside. Specialized nets for hammocks, cots, and small beds are also available. Mosquito coils are a well-known example of insecticide vaporizers, typically containing synthetic pyrethroids as the active ingredient. More advanced products, such as insecticide mats placed on electrically heated grids, release insecticide vapor and require electricity. Battery-operated vaporizers are also available. These devices can be used during the daytime if necessary. Aerosol sprays designed to kill flying insects are effective for quick knockdown and killing. Indoor sleeping areas should be sprayed before bedtime. Treating a room with an insecticide spray can help eliminate insects, though the effect may be short-lived. Combining spraying with the use of a vaporizer or mosquito net is recommended. Protective clothing can also reduce exposure to vectors during their active periods. The thickness of the material is important. Insect repellents applied to clothing are effective for longer durations than when applied to the skin. Additional protection can be achieved by treating clothing with permethrin or etofenprox to prevent mosquito bites through the fabric. In areas infested with ticks and fleas, appropriate footwear and tucking long trousers into socks are recommended. These measures can be further enhanced by applying repellents to clothing. Travelers camping in tents should use a combination of mosquito repellents and screens. Special mosquito screens with a mesh size of less than 5 mm are necessary. Screening of windows, doors, and eaves reduces exposure to flying insects, and accommodations with these features should be prioritized. Air-conditioning is a highly effective method of keeping mosquitoes and other insects out of a room, provided there are no gaps around windows or doors. In air-conditioned hotels, additional precautions are generally unnecessary indoors. Vector-borne diseases are caused by various pathogens transmitted by specific vectors. For example, Aedes mosquitoes transmit viral diseases such as chikungunya, dengue, yellow fever, Zika, and Rift Valley fever. Anopheles mosquitoes are vectors for parasitic diseases like malaria and lymphatic filariasis. Culex mosquitoes transmit Japanese encephalitis, West Nile fever, and lymphatic filariasis. Other vectors include aquatic snails (schistosomiasis), blackflies (onchocerciasis), fleas (plague and tungiasis), lice (typhus and relapsing fever), sandflies (leishmaniasis and sandfly fever), ticks (Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, Lyme disease, tick-borne encephalitis, and tularemia), triatomine bugs (Chagas disease), and tsetse flies (sleeping sickness). Insecticide-treated bed nets have been shown to significantly reduce malaria-related deaths. In some communities, additional measures, such as impregnating reed mats with insecticide and hanging them on walls, are employed to kill mosquitoes.
